items.title: Advanced evals: finding the AI failures you don't know about
items.summary: Lenny's newsletter walks through error discovery — systematically surfacing hidden failure modes in an AI product before writing eval criteria, so your metrics measure real problems instead of imagined ones.
items.why: You ship agents; evals are the PM skill that separates demo-grade from production-grade. Error discovery is the step most teams skip.

cards.back: Reading real outputs/traces to find actual failure modes first, then turning those into eval criteria — instead of guessing metrics up front.

cards.front: Why not start with a metric?
cards.back: Predefined metrics miss failure modes you haven't imagined; you optimize for what you measured, not what breaks.
A domain expert or PM who can judge 'good' — it's judgment work, not just engineering.

quiz.q: According to the eval workflow, what should come first?
options: Pick a scoring metric and benchmark
Look at real outputs to discover failure modes
Fine-tune the model
Add more tools to the agent
quiz.why: Error discovery precedes criteria: you can only measure failures you've actually found.

items.title: Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Sol and Luna land — plus a 40-50% price war
items.summary: Simon Willison rounds up a chaotic release week: Anthropic's Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol/Luna arrive within a day of each other, alongside Grok 4.7, with frontier prices cut sharply.
items.why: Your model choice and unit economics just changed. Worth re-running cost assumptions for your Bedrock agents this week.

cards.front: What changed in the frontier model lineup this week?
cards.back: Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Sol and Luna, and Grok 4.7 all shipped within ~48 hours, with price cuts of roughly 40-50%.

cards.front: Why do model price cuts matter to a PM?
cards.back: They change per-request cost, so features that were too expensive (bigger context, more agent steps, more retries) can become viable.

quiz.q: What was the main commercial story alongside the Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 launches?
options: Frontier model prices dropped roughly 40-50%
Open weights were discontinued
API rate limits were removed
All labs moved to per-seat pricing
quiz.why: Competing releases triggered a price war, reshaping cost models for agent products.

items.title: Warp's 'AI factory': 2,000 PRs a month from Slack and Linear tickets
items.summary: Warp's CEO explains a pipeline that turns requests from Slack, Linear and GitHub into tested, tracked pull requests run by cloud agents — and how the team measures and improves that pipeline over time.

items.title: Why Opus 5.5 won back a user who'd quit Claude

items.title: Claude Opus 5.5 is live on Amazon Bedrock
items.summary: Anthropic's most capable agentic-coding model is now available on Bedrock and Claude Platform on AWS, with guidance on when to use it for long-running tasks and how to start calling it.

items.why: The Bedrock-native counterpart to Lenny's evals piece — concrete tooling for evaluating the agents your team already runs.

items.title: How I AI weekly: Meta's Muse reviewed, plus the Warp factory episode
items.summary: The week's How I AI roundup pairs a hands-on review of Meta's Muse with the Warp AI-factory conversation, aimed at PMs wanting to see real AI workflows rather than product announcements.

weekly.headline: A frontier release week (Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Sol and Luna) plus a price war — and evals become the PM skill that matters
weekly.script:
Big week. Two things collided: new frontier models, and a fresh push on how we actually judge them.

Start with evals. Lenny's newsletter published a piece on advanced evals, and the key idea is error discovery: before you write a single scoring criterion, you go hunting for the failure modes you don't know your product has. Most teams invert this — they invent metrics first and end up measuring imaginary problems. For you, shipping agents, this is the line between a demo that impresses and something that survives real users.

Second, Simon Willison rounded up a chaotic release week. Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol and Luna landed within a day of each other, Grok 4.7 alongside them, and frontier prices dropped roughly forty to fifty percent. That means your cost assumptions for your Bedrock agents are stale. Re-run the math this week; things you priced out as too expensive may now be affordable.

Third, and conveniently: Opus 5.5 is already live on Amazon Bedrock. That's your exact stack — Lambda plus Bedrock — so testing it in a production agent is a config change, not a migration.

Fourth, Lenny ran blind head-to-head tests of Opus 5.5 versus GPT-6 Sol across six task types: writing, frontend prototypes, long-running agentic tasks, SVGs, coding and video editing. The lesson isn't which model won; it's the method. Pick models per task from your own blind tests, not from benchmark press releases.

Fifth, AWS published a guide to evaluating skill-equipped agents using Strands Evals with Bedrock AgentCore. It measures whether your agent picked the right skill and followed instructions — not just whether the answer sounded fluent. That's the native tooling twin of Lenny's evals piece.

One bonus: Warp's CEO described an AI factory turning Slack and Linear tickets into two thousand pull requests a month. Worth stealing the operating model for Bitbucket.

cards.back: Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol and Luna arrived within about a day of each other, with Grok 4.7 alongside — and frontier prices were cut roughly 40–50%.

cards.front: Why the price cuts matter for a Bedrock team
cards.back: Per-token costs drive agent unit economics. A ~40–50% frontier price drop changes which workloads are affordable, so cost models, routing rules and 'too expensive' decisions should be re-run.

Lenny compared Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol blind across six task types (writing, frontend prototypes, long agentic runs, SVGs, coding, video editing). Takeaway: choose models per task from your own blind tests, not benchmarks.
AWS tooling for judging agents on whether they selected the correct skill and followed instructions — because a fluent-sounding answer doesn't prove the right procedure was used.

quiz.q: According to this week's Lenny piece on advanced evals, what should happen before you write eval criteria?
options: Error discovery — surfacing failure modes you don't yet know about
Pick a benchmark like SWE-bench and track it
Fine-tune the model on your own data
Run an A/B test on pricing
quiz.why: Criteria written before discovery tend to measure imagined problems; discovery grounds them in real observed failures.

quiz.q: What happened to frontier model pricing during this release week?
options: Prices rose about 20% due to demand
Prices were cut roughly 40–50%
Pricing moved from per-token to per-seat
Pricing was unchanged
quiz.why: Simon Willison's roundup notes sharp cuts of about 40–50% alongside the Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 launches.

quiz.q: What do Strands Evals with Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations primarily measure?
options: How fluent and well-written the agent's response is
Token cost per request
Whether the agent chose the right skill and followed instructions
How fast the model returns its first token
quiz.why: The point is that fluency isn't proof of correct procedure, so the evals target skill selection and instruction-following.
